title: India’s Monsoon Has Arrived. The Forecast Says It May Not Be Enough.
excerpt: The southwest monsoon reached Kerala three days late. With an 84 percent chance of below-normal rainfall and El Niño building, India’s farms and food prices face their toughest season in a decade.
body:
India’s southwest monsoon officially reached Kerala on June 4, three days behind its normal June 1 schedule, bringing relief from a punishing heatwave that had pushed power demand to record highs across the country. But the delayed onset is the least of the worries for a nation that depends on these four months of rain for nearly everything — food, water, and a significant share of economic output.

The India Meteorological Department confirmed the monsoon has covered all of Kerala and advanced into parts of Tamil Nadu and coastal Karnataka. Conditions are favorable for further progress into Goa and Maharashtra’s Konkan coast over the coming days, with widespread coverage of the western seaboard expected by mid-June.

## The El Niño Factor

What makes this monsoon season different is the shadow of El Niño hanging over it. In its updated long-range forecast released May 29, the IMD projected that total monsoon rainfall would reach only 90 percent of the long-period average of 87 centimeters — the lowest in 11 years. The probability breakdown is stark: there is a 60 percent chance of deficient rainfall and a 24 percent chance of below-normal rainfall. Together, that is an 84 percent probability that India will receive less rain than it needs.

The World Meteorological Organization has reinforced this outlook, estimating an 80 percent chance that El Niño conditions will develop between June and August, with a 90 percent probability of the pattern persisting through at least November. Climate scientists are warning that this could be one of the strongest El Niño events on record, with sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific potentially exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius above average.

## What It Means for Farmers and Food Prices

The monsoon delivers roughly 70 percent of India’s annual rainfall and is the lifeline for crops including rice, corn, cotton, soybeans, and sugarcane. With only about 55 percent of India’s farmland under irrigation, the remaining acreage is entirely at the mercy of the rains.

Across Asia, the effects are already visible. Reuters reported that hot weather and below-normal rains are disrupting planting from India’s northwestern grain belt to Thailand’s rice paddies and Indonesia’s palm oil plantations. Global wheat prices have climbed about 20 percent since January, and rice prices at major Southeast Asian hubs have risen roughly 15 percent over the past month.

For Indian farmers, the timing is doubly painful. El Niño-driven dryness arrives alongside fertilizer and diesel shortages caused by the Iran war’s disruption of trade routes through the Strait of Hormuz. The IMD has flagged that the Monsoon Core Zone — the rainfed agriculture belt that stretches across central India — is most likely to see below-normal rainfall this season.

## The Macro Picture

The RBI’s own June 2026 projections reflect the anxiety. Retail inflation has been revised upward to an average of 5.1 percent for the fiscal year, up from 4.6 percent, with food prices expected to be a primary driver. GDP growth has been trimmed to 6.6 percent from 6.9 percent.

Economists at ICRA, HDFC Bank, and Kotak Mahindra Bank have all warned that weak monsoons, combined with elevated energy costs from the Middle East conflict, could drag growth below 6.5 percent in the second half of the fiscal year. ICRA chief economist Aditi Nayar has not ruled out a rate hike as early as the third quarter of FY2027.

## The Diaspora Connection

For NRIs sending remittances home, the monsoon matters more than it might seem. A poor harvest season drives up food prices, erodes the purchasing power of families in India, and increases the financial pressure on diaspora households that supplement rural incomes. With the rupee already down 5 percent this year and crude oil above $90 a barrel, every dollar sent home buys less than it did six months ago.

India’s monsoon season has always been a gamble. This year, the odds are worse than usual — and the stakes, in an already turbulent global economy, are considerably higher.
